Police said the vehicle had struck multiple ⁠people after being driven into the Tiergarten. Shortly before 10pm the driver of the white minivan swerved into the park, close to where the route of the Pride march had been earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree.

Bild cited a witness as saying that a man had emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot. A hunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.

Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in Berlin in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the Pride parade. It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.

Berlin’s mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.

The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “taking a stand is hot”, which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to LGBTQ+ people in Germany.

More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.

Before last year’s parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisations sounded the alarm that attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat. Campaigners said a rise in hostility had accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.

Far-right leaders were also quick to comment on the attacks. The co-leader of the AfD Tino Chrupalla wrote on X: “We declare the war against Islamists. We will not allow religious extremists to divide our country with violence and intolerance!”

The president of the French far-right National Rally, Jordan Bardella, wrote: “The Islamist threat remains a major issue in Europe and continues to target what they hate most about our civilisation – and what we cherish so much – freedom.”

ولا تمثل المعطيات الواردة في هذه الورقة سوى الحد الأدنى مما أمكن توثيقه، في ظل استمرار الاحتلال في إخفاء الآلاف من معتقلي قطاع غزة قسراً، ومنع المؤسسات الدولية والحقوقية من الوصول إليهم، الأمر الذي يجعل حجم الجرائم والانتهاكات داخل السجون والمعسكرات أكبر بكثير مما تسمح ظروف التوثيق الراهنة بكشفه.⁩

🇷🇺 Russia's fuel deficit is gradually easing across Moscow and the regions — queues are shrinking and gas stations are relaxing limits, though shortages persist in several areas.

In Moscow, most fuel grades are available, with only minor queuing. Gazprom Neft stations formally cap app purchases at 30L, but full tank fills are common at the register — Teboil and many Lukoil stations have no limits at all. Prices remain largely stable.

Leningrad Region and St. Petersburg: Lukoil has lifted limits entirely; Rosneft and Bashneft raised caps to 50L. Astrakhan, Volgograd, Rostov, Krasnodar, and Stavropol regions, plus the M-4 highway, are also limit-free — restrictions remain in Vladimir, Voronezh, Kaluga, Lipetsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Oryol, and Tula regions. Omsk Region lifted its limits entirely.

Crimea is seeing gradual normalization, though TES and ATAN stations still won't honor previously purchased fuel vouchers and cards for most customers, reserving supply for emergency and social services. In the DPR, shortages and elevated prices (~2.5x Moscow levels) persist, with continued queues and restrictions.

Price spread remains wide: AI-95 runs ~72-75 rubles/liter in Moscow, ~72-81 in Rostov-on-Don, ~120-180 in Simferopol, and 180-190 in Donetsk (diesel 180-200).

Russian officials cite the export ban through year-end, boosted production, delayed refinery maintenance, and restored capacity at drone-struck plants — plus contracted imports, including from India. The core driver, though, appears to be refineries damaged by strikes coming back online, with fewer new refinery hits reported recently — the most recent being Tyumen refinery, which Reuters reports has since halted operations. Russian air defense has improved, though it's also possible Ukraine has simply lowered the intensity of strikes on refineries in favor of other targets (like Wildberries warehouses).

The trajectory from here hinges on whether Ukraine can keep striking major refineries or whether Russia stabilizes capacity — though a repeat crisis this autumn will be harder to trigger once the summer consumption peak passes.
